name: Java Virtual Machine (HotSpot)
summary: The abstract machine that runs Java bytecode, and OpenJDK’s HotSpot, the implementation most people use: an interpreter, two JIT compilers and a choice of garbage collectors behind Java, Scala, Clojure and other languages.
intro: The JVM is defined by a specification, not by one program. It knows nothing of the Java language, only of the `class` file format: bytecode for a stack machine plus a symbol table. Any language that can be expressed as valid class files can run on it, which is how Scala and Clojure share Java’s libraries. The specification also leaves the garbage collector open: objects live on a heap shared by all threads and are “never explicitly deallocated”, but how the heap is collected is up to the implementation.

HotSpot, the JVM in OpenJDK, has a class loader, a bytecode interpreter, two or three JIT compilers and a handful of garbage collectors, in more than 1.2 million lines of C and C++. A method starts out interpreted. With tiered compilation, on by default, methods that run often are compiled first by the client compiler into code that records a profile of itself, then by the server compiler, which uses that profile to optimise. For memory, G1 is the default collector on most machines; ZGC keeps pauses under a millisecond at some cost in throughput, and the serial collector suits heaps up to about 100 MB. Since Java 21, virtual threads let a server run one cheap thread per request instead of one OS thread.

Start-up is the JVM’s weak spot, and two projects attack it. JDK 24 can record which classes an app loads and links in a training run and keep them, already loaded and linked, in an ahead-of-time cache; Spring PetClinic then starts in 2.604 seconds instead of 4.486. GraalVM Native Image goes all the way: it analyses which code is reachable and compiles the app ahead of time into a native executable that starts in milliseconds, as long as every class it needs is known at build time.
strengths: Compile once: the same class files run on every operating system and CPU that has a JVM
A profile-guided JIT: tiered compilation starts fast with the client compiler and reaches peak speed with the server compiler
A choice of garbage collectors, from serial for small heaps to G1 by default and ZGC for sub-millisecond pauses
One runtime for many languages: Java, Scala and Clojure share libraries, and `invokedynamic` (Java 7) helps dynamically typed languages run efficiently
Virtual threads (Java 21) make thread-per-request servers cheap without rewriting code as callbacks
limits: Slow start and warm-up: a large app loads and links tens of thousands of classes (about 21,000 for Spring PetClinic) and runs interpreted until the JIT catches up
Memory overhead beyond the heap: tiered compilation alone multiplies the default code cache size by five
Ahead-of-time compilation with Native Image assumes a closed world, so reflection and dynamic class loading need metadata at build time
Low-pause collectors cost throughput: ZGC trades some throughput for its sub-millisecond pauses

story: Sun designed the Java platform for networked consumer devices, where “compiled code had to survive transport across networks, operate on any client, and assure the client that it was safe to run.” The answer was a virtual machine with its own instruction set and strict checks on the code it loads. The first prototype JVM ran on a handheld device that resembled a PDA, the HotJava browser showed programs downloaded with web pages, and JDK 1.0 shipped on 23 January 1996.

Early JVMs were slow. In 1997 Sun bought Animorphic (Longview Technologies), founded by Urs Hölzle and Lars Bak from Sun’s cancelled Self project, whose Strongtalk virtual machine compiled only the code that ran often. Sun built HotSpot on that work, with a new optimising server compiler started by Cliff Click, and released it on 27 April 1999, claiming it doubled the performance of Java 2.

On 13 November 2006 Sun released HotSpot and the Java compiler under the GPL, the start of OpenJDK, which has been the reference implementation of Java SE since version 7. Oracle took over when it bought Sun. Since then the JVM has kept growing in two directions: more languages (`invokedynamic` for dynamic languages in JDK 7, July 2011) and new runtime features such as virtual threads (JDK 21, September 2023) and an ahead-of-time class cache (JDK 24, March 2025).

choices.choice: A portable bytecode with strict checks
choices.why: Code arrived over the network from strangers. The JVM imposes strong syntactic and structural constraints on class files so it can refuse unsafe code before running it, on any host.

choices.choice: Interpret first, compile the hot spots
choices.why: HotSpot’s name says it: profile the running program and spend compiler time only where it runs most. Tiered compilation later added a quick first compiler so start-up no longer had to wait for the server compiler.
The specification “assumes no particular type of automatic storage management”, so HotSpot could add new collectors, from serial to G1 and ZGC, without changing a line of anyone’s bytecode.
Besides the JVM’s own bootstrap loader, applications can supply their own class loaders to change how classes are found and loaded, which lets servers and plugins load code at run time.
